(Tuesday through next Sunday)
Issued at 133 PM CDT Sun Sep 27 2026

The strong trough now moving ashore the West Coast will start to 
shape the weather over our area as we head further into the week. 
Its approach will impinge on the ridging near our area and 
eventually shove the ridge eastward. On Tuesday, the trough is 
forecast to push into the southwestern US. There will still be 
enough ridging over Texas to keep conditions dry and hot for much of 
the day, but increasing onshore flow in response to jet divergence 
caused by the trough raises chances for isolated streamer showers 
over the Coastal Plains.

Along the leading flanks of the incoming trough, a substantial plume 
of tropical Pacific moisture will begin flowing across Mexico up 
into South-Central Texas beginning about late Tuesday, and should 
continue to do so through at least Thursday with additional 
contributions from onshore flow off the Gulf. This pattern sets the 
stage for potential widespread rain during the latter half of the 
week. There is still some variation in timing with the EPS ensembles 
generally favoring a slower progression and the GEFS and CMCE 
ensembles being faster, but the overall depiction of at least the 
start and midpoint of the rainy period is coming into better 
agreement. Rain chances start to increase Wednesday areawide as 
the southerly low-level jet establishes over the region, making 
for an especially humid and breezy day. However, at this range it
does appear that Wednesday's activity will be more in the form of
scattered showers embedded in the moist flow off the Gulf. A 
Pacific cold front acting to concentrate the rain and storm 
potential will then slowly enter our area from the northwest. The 
current consensus among the more skillful models suggests heavy 
frontal rains could commence as early as Wednesday night, slowly 
advancing east during the night and throughout the day Thursday. 
Risks of excessive rainfall capable of causing flash flooding 
applies to all of South-Central Texas during this period. While 
it's still early to give more specific rain amounts and ranges, 
models have been consistent in showing a band of heavier amounts 
on a roughly NNE- to-SSW swath, paralleling the orientation of the
slow- moving front. These rains will have access to ample amounts
of atmospheric moisture, to the tune of widespread PWATs in 
excess of 2" as depicted on the latest ensemble means (at or above
the 95th percentile). These signals are supportive of a heavy 
rain event, and we will continue to closely monitor the 
development of the trough and its front for trends as we enter the
workweek.

The greatest overlap in rain chances in the latest models is around 
Thursday, though that is subject to change depending on how the 
trough evolves. While there are some deterministic models that clear 
the front and its rains out of our area at a steady pace, more 
models have trended towards showing the parent trough slowing down 
and even stalling over the central and southern Plains. This may 
keep the front and rain potential in our area into Friday, an 
outcome best exemplified by the EPS and ML versions of the ECMWF 
and GFS. We do generally expect that the mid- and upper-level flow
will become more zonal over the weekend, breaking up the moisture
plume and allowing drier air to finally make its way into the 
area. The rain forecast for the weekend is uncertain and heavily 
dependent on how quickly the trough leaves the area, but for now, 
a gradual decrease in rain chances is depicted.

Temperatures to start the week will be unseasonably warm. The 
combination of humid air and hot temperatures Wednesday afternoon 
could may that day especially sultry if clouds from the approaching 
front are delayed. Higher heat indices near and over 105F are 
possible over the Rio Grande Plains and portions of the I-35 
corridor and Coastal Plains. The Pacific cold front and widespread 
rain and cloud cover should bring daytime temperatures down Thursday 
into the weekend, with highs in the 80s becoming more widespread. In 
the longer term, there have been some indications that a cold front 
could bring cooler weather next week. I wouldn't count too heavily 
on that, but it does appear that more opportunities for fall-like 
temperatures may be on tap through early October.
